claims.text: The AlCoCrFeNi-based eutectic high-entropy alloy has a distinct dual-phase morphology.
Its interphase boundaries are inherently prone to passive-film breakdown.
Mechanical wear preferentially disrupts native passive films at chemically heterogeneous interphase boundaries.
Disruption of the passive film exposes less corrosion-resistant phases.
At approximately 600°C, enhanced oxidation kinetics and diffusion accelerate localized oxidation at interphase boundaries.
Microgalvanic coupling between phases contributes to localized oxidation or corrosion at the interphase boundaries.
Localized corrosion reduces hardness and cohesion near the interphase boundaries.
Reduced local hardness and cohesion increase the wear rate.
Increased wear creates new reactive sites and thereby promotes further corrosion.
A uniform, adherent, and thermally stable pre-formed oxide layer at interphase boundaries will shield those boundaries during tribocorrosion.
Pre-passivation will interrupt the proposed cyclical wear-corrosion degradation mechanism.
Relative to the untreated baseline, the pre-passivated sample will exhibit lower total synergistic degradation.
Relative to the untreated baseline, the pre-passivated sample will have a lower wear rate.
Relative to the untreated baseline, the pre-passivated sample will have a lower corrosion rate.
The proposed mechanism is especially relevant near 600°C and in chloride-containing or similarly aggressive environments.
The comparison will hold mechanical load, sliding speed, temperature, and corrosive environment constant between untreated and pre-passivated samples.

contradictions.description: The conditions alternatively specify a chloride-containing molten-salt electrolyte or a simulated oxidizing atmosphere, but corrosion-current measurements by electrochemical methods are not directly applicable to both environments without distinct cell configurations.

The boundary conditions assume that the passivation layer remains stable under wear, whereas the falsification rule treats failure of that layer to remain intact as falsification of the interphase microgalvanic mechanism. Coating failure instead violates the intervention assumption and does not by itself refute the proposed underlying mechanism.
